newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech stats bureau revises fcasts as economy slides.
newsitem.headline: Czech stats bureau revises fcasts as economy slides.

text.p: The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) on Friday revised most of its major economic indicators, reflecting the worsening state of the country's economy.

The CSU cut its estimate for real GDP growth in 1997 to between 2.9-3.5 percent, from a previous 4-5 percent forecast, while it said average annual inflation should finish the year at 8.2-8.8 percent, revised up from 7.5-8.0 percent.

A CSU statement said that the GDP growth forecast had been reduced for several reasons including continued slow economic growth in Germany, the country's largest trading partner in the West, and the rise of the crown early in the year which made imports cheaper and hurt exports.

It added that the central bank's tight monetary policy, implemented last summer, also had an influence on slowing economic growth, as did a railway strike in February and poor weather which has hurt construction output. "These influences are temporary and will weaken," the statement said.
"It may be expected that, after a significant slowdown in the first quarter of 1997, GDP will, step-by-step, come back to 'normal' growth rates...approximately 4-5 percent," it added.
Real GDP grew by 4.4 percent, year-on-year in 1996.

For inflation, the CSU said a series of deregulations of energy prices and rent should force inflation well above current levels, but that the benefits of slowing growth in the money supply and wages should help pull the rate back down by the end of the year.

"It should be assumed that inflation will grow namely in reflection to prepared deregulations of prices of housing, heating, electricity and gas...when the (average) inflation rate may temporarily reach around 10 percent," it said.
The average inflation rate in 1996 was 8.8 percent, while the average rate as of March was 8.4 percent.
After industrial production contracted in the first two months of 1997, the CSU revised its full-year prediction to 3-5 percent.

One of the few favourbale revisions the CSU made was to its trade deficit estimate, which it revised downward to 190-200 billion crowns from a previous 202-212 billion. The 1996 trade gap was 159.8 billion crowns.

The CSU said the strength of the crown, which hit a record high of +5.51 percent against the mid-point of its dollar/mark basket at the beginning of February, had negatively affected the trade balance in the first quarter.
But the crown has since fallen sharply to 2.0-3.0 percent below basket parity, where it is expected to stay for several months and help the trade deficit.

The CSU said it expects exports to rise by some 4.5-6.5 percent for 1997, unchanged from its previous estimate, but that imports would grow 7.5-10.5 percent, a revision downward from its previous estimate of 9-12 percent import growth.
"We have reduced our forecast for the growth of imports...especially with respect to the introduction of import deposits," the statement said.
Under the deposit scheme adpoted by the government on April 21, importers will be required to deposit 20 percent of the value of imported consumer goods on an interest-free account for 180 days.
The statement said that given the government's recent limiting of public sector wage growth to 7.3 percent from an initial target of 11.9 percent, nominal wage growth should be less-than-expected.

The CSU said that after wage growth of 18 percent in 1996, 1997 nominal wages should rise by between 14-15.5 percent, down from its previous estimate of 14.5-126.5 percent. It added that in 1998, wage growth should ease again to 13-15 percent.
It said the unemployment rate by the end of 1997 should be between 3.6-4.0 percent, and "with an outlook on (industrial) restructuring, we expect the 1998 (figure) to rise to 4-5 percent".
The unemployment rate at the end of 1996 was 3.5 percent, and 3.9 percent at the end of March.
-- Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
